pl-l3d15c1-d1e117.summary: States that the Son of God took a passible human nature, a passible soul and passible, mortal flesh: to prove he had a true body he took bodily defects such as hunger and thirst; to prove he had a true soul he took the soul's defects, sorrow, fear, pain, and the like.
claims: Christ assumed passible soul and flesh.
Christ's defects prove the reality of his body and soul.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e120.summary: States that all sensation belongs to the soul: the flesh does not sense, but the soul using the body as an instrument.
claims: All sensation belongs to the soul using the body.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e123.summary: Cites Augustine, Literal Commentary on Genesis XII: the body does not sense, but the soul through the body, which it uses as a messenger. As the soul sees and hears through the body as an instrument, so through the body it feels some evils it would not feel without it, like hunger and thirst, rightly called defects of the body; others it feels without the body, like fear. So the soul feels pains, some through the body, some not.
claims: The soul senses through the body as instrument.
Some pains are felt through the body, others not.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e136.summary: States that Christ took true human defects as he took true human nature, but not all: defects of penalty, not of guilt, and not all of those, only those it was expedient for man that he take and that did not derogate from his dignity. As he became man for man's sake, so he took man's defects for man's sake: he took of ours to give us of his, took our oldness to pour his newness into us; he took the single oldness of penalty to consume our double oldness of penalty and guilt.
claims: Christ took defects of penalty, not guilt.
Christ took only defects that were expedient and fitting.
Christ's single penalty consumes our double penalty and guilt.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e142.summary: Qualifies the authority that Christ took all our weaknesses except sin: this is false unless restricted to those he ought to take for us and that did not dishonor him. He did not take ignorance, though there is a kind that is a defect and not a sin, invincible ignorance (vincible ignorance is sin, at least about things we should know; ignorance of things not relevant to salvation may not be a defect). Ignorance and difficulty in willing or doing good pertain to our misery.
claims: Christ did not take all our weaknesses but only fitting ones.
Christ did not take ignorance.
Invincible ignorance is a defect but not a sin; vincible ignorance is sin.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e145.summary: Cites Augustine, De libero arbitrio III: approving false for true and erring unwillingly, and being unable to restrain oneself from lustful works because of the flesh's chain, is not the nature of man as created but the penalty of the condemned; from this misery God's grace frees, since man could fall by free choice but not rise. Ignorance and difficulty, which every man suffers from birth, belong to this misery. So these are penalties of man, which Christ did not have; so he did not take all defects of our weakness except sin.
claims: Ignorance and difficulty are penalties of fallen man.
Christ did not have ignorance and difficulty.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e160.summary: Anticipates the reply that ignorance and difficulty are themselves sins.
claims: Objection: ignorance and difficulty are sins.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e163.summary: Opposes this with Augustine's Retractations: even if ignorance and difficulty were man's natural beginnings, God would be praised, not blamed, implying God could have placed them in man blamelessly before sin. But if man had them by nature at the start, would they be defects and penalties? If a penalty were placed in him before sin, it would seem unjust that he felt penalty before guilt.
claims: God could blamelessly have created man with ignorance and difficulty.
Penalty before guilt would be unjust.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e175.summary: Answers that they would not have been defects or penalties had they been natural, as being unable to advance was no defect for man before sin when he had not yet received grace; but after he received grace, advanced for a time, and lost it by his fault along with the ability to advance, inability to avoid evil and do good became defect and penalty. So Christ took all our defects except sin that were fitting for him and expedient for us, being wholly free of many diseases and bodily flaws. He took fear and sorrow to show true humanity, passibility and mortality to accomplish his work, and death to raise our hope from despair of immortality.
claims: Ignorance and difficulty would not be penalties if natural.
Christ took only defects fitting for him and expedient for us.
Christ's defects serve to show his humanity, accomplish his work, and raise our hope.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e179.summary: Adds that he took these defects not by necessity of his condition but by will of mercy. He had real defects as we do, but not for the same cause: we contract them from original sin, as Rom 8:10 says the body is dead because of sin, i.e., has the necessity of dying. Christ was conceived, born, and lived without sin, and transferred true weakness from us to himself by mercy alone, as he took true flesh, which he could have assumed without any weakness, just as he took it without guilt.
claims: Christ's defects were taken by will, not necessity.
We contract defects from original sin; Christ did not.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e188.summary: Introduces proofs against some who wrongly held that the man Christ bore only the likeness and image of suffering and pain but felt no pain or suffering at all.
claims: Some held Christ felt no real pain.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e191.summary: Cites Isaiah: surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our sorrows (Is 53:4).
claims: Christ bore our infirmities and sorrows.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e197.summary: Cites the Gospel: 'my soul is sorrowful unto death' (Mt 26:38) and 'Jesus began to fear and be weary' (Mk 14:33).
claims: Christ was sorrowful and afraid.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e206.summary: Cites Ps 87:4, 'my soul is filled with evils', with Augustine's comment: Christ's soul was filled not with vices and sins but with human evils, sorrows, by which it suffered with the flesh; bodily pain cannot exist without the soul, but the soul can grieve without the body's pain. He took these affections of human weakness, like flesh and death, by will of mercy, not necessity.
claims: Christ's soul was filled with human sorrows, not sins.
Christ took these affections by will of mercy.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e218.summary: Cites Ambrose, De Trinitate: 'Father, if possible, let this cup pass from me': Christ fears; while Peter does not fear, Christ does. Peter said 'I will lay down my life for you', Christ says 'my soul is troubled'. Both are true: the lesser does not fear, and the greater bears the affection of one who fears.
claims: Christ truly bore the affection of fear.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e237.summary: Adds Ambrose: as man he is troubled, weeps, is crucified; through human nature he was weary and rose. His power and divinity are not troubled, but his soul is, through assuming human frailty; who took a soul took also the soul's passion, for as God he could not be troubled or die.
claims: Christ was troubled as man, not as God.
Who takes a soul takes its passion.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e249.summary: Adds Ambrose: he took my sorrow; I boldly name sorrow, since I preach the cross. As man he had sorrow, which he took with my affection; he suffers with me, is sorrowful and grieves for me, having nothing for himself to grieve. You grieve, Lord Jesus, my wounds, not yours.
claims: Christ grieved for us, not for himself.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e258.summary: Cites Jerome's Explanation of the faith: the passible man was taken by the Son so that the deity remained impassible; the Son suffered truly, not in appearance, all that Scripture says, according to what could suffer, the assumed substance. The Son's person took a passible man, yet by its own substance suffered nothing, like the whole impassible Trinity.
claims: Christ suffered truly in the assumed substance.
The deity remained impassible.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e270.summary: Concludes that these and other authorities make clear that Christ assumed a truly passible man and took in it the defects and affections of our weakness, but by will, not by necessity of condition.
claims: Christ truly took passible humanity with its defects and affections.
He did so by will, not necessity.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e273.summary: Notes that some passages in the saints' treatises seem to contradict this.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e276.summary: Cites Augustine on Ps 21:3 as seeming to say Christ neither truly feared nor was truly sad: how could the sinless one say this? He speaks for us, his body the Church, as when he said 'let this cup pass from me', unless he is thought to have feared death; but the Lord did not truly fear suffering, to rise on the third day, when Paul longed to be dissolved and be with Christ. The soldier is not braver than the commander; he spoke representing our weakness, for his weak ones who fear death.
claims: Augustine seems to say Christ did not truly fear death.
Christ spoke in the person of his body, the Church.

pl-l3d15c1-d1e295.summary: Cites Jerome: let those blush who think the Savior feared death and said 'let this cup pass' from dread of the passion.
claims: Jerome seems to deny that Christ feared death.

pl-l3d15c1.summary: Teaches that the Son assumed a passible nature: passible soul and passible, mortal flesh, with bodily defects (hunger, thirst) to prove a true body and defects of soul (sorrow, fear, pain) to prove a true soul. All sensation belongs to the soul using the body. Christ assumed defects of penalty, not guilt, and not all of them, only those fitting for us and not unbecoming to his dignity: not ignorance or difficulty in doing good, which belong to our misery. He took them by will of mercy, not necessity of condition, unlike us who contract them from original sin. Against those who say he felt no real pain, Isaiah, the Gospels, Augustine, Ambrose, and Jerome show that he truly suffered, feared, and grieved. Yet some texts of Augustine and Jerome seem to deny he truly feared death.
claims: Christ assumed a passible soul and passible, mortal flesh.
Christ assumed defects of penalty but not of guilt, and only those fitting.
Christ did not assume ignorance or difficulty in doing good.
Christ took on defects by will of mercy, not by necessity.
Christ truly felt pain, fear, and sorrow.
